From extermination…
to singing the national anthem in their own language.
These are the Indigenous peoples of El Salvador.
In 1932, the army killed thousands of them.
And it picked them out by their clothes and their language.
Ninety-three years later, in the Assembly of Bukele's party, a group of children from Izalco sang the anthem in Nahuat.
It was the first time.
What happened in between?
And what has changed under Bukele?
First, coffee.
With it, the Indigenous towns of the west had been losing their communal lands.
On the night of January 22, 1932, the peasants, mostly Indigenous Nahua, rose up.
They took Izalco, Nahuizalco, Juayúa, Tacuba…
They wanted back the land they had lost.
With them were Farabundo Martí's Communist Party and Indigenous leaders like Feliciano Ama, from Izalco.
Three days later, the army had retaken every town.
And then began what El Salvador simply calls «la Matanza», the Massacre.
General Maximiliano Hernández Martínez was in power.
For about two weeks, his soldiers shot anyone who looked Indigenous: by the way they dressed, by the way they spoke.
Feliciano Ama was hanged in the square of Izalco.
How many died?
No one knows exactly.
At least ten thousand, according to historians Gould and Lauria-Santiago.
Others say up to thirty thousand.
Guadalupe Estrada was born in Sonsonate in 1948, sixteen years after the Massacre.
According to the caption of her portrait, the wounds 1932 left on her family led her to say out loud that she is Indigenous.
Many families did the opposite.
Women put away the refajo skirt and the huipil.
Parents stopped speaking Nahuat to their children.
Fear was enough.
Speaking it outside the home was shameful.
And frightening.
Anastacia López, from Santo Domingo de Guzmán, did learn it at home.
Spanish, she says, she learned at nine.
Today, those who learned Nahuat as children, like her, are very few.
Almost all of them elderly.
It was 2010.
President Mauricio Funes apologized to the Indigenous peoples for the «persecution and extermination».
The word from the beginning.
It was the first time.
Four years later, the Constitution changed one sentence: «El Salvador recognizes Indigenous peoples».
Then came Nayib Bukele.
With him as president, the Assembly declared August 9 the National Day of Indigenous Peoples.
Unanimously.
In that Assembly the anthem was sung in Nahuat.
And the following year, another school sang it there again.
And the census asked something simple again: are you Indigenous?
In 2007, thirteen thousand people said yes.
How many, seventeen years later?
Sixty-eight thousand.
Five times more.
And about eleven hundred people say they speak Nahuat, according to the 2024 census.
They would all fit in one large theater.
What hasn't come:
No president has apologized again since 2010.
The State has not investigated 1932.
A law on Indigenous peoples has still not been passed.
And El Salvador has not signed the UN convention that protects these peoples, number 169.
They're called Cunas Náhuat, Nahuat nests.
Children aged three to five spend the whole day in Nahuat, without a word of Spanish.
The teachers are grandmothers who learned it as girls.
They call them nantzin.
The first one opened in 2010, in Santo Domingo de Guzmán.
More than six hundred children have gone through them.
In 2023, the Ministry of Education moved the Cunas Náhuat into its new program, without consulting the communities.
Of thirteen teachers, five were left.
The grandmothers and the towns reopened them, with help from abroad.
Young people first.
Twenty-five teenagers from Santo Domingo, aged fifteen to seventeen, learned to film their elders so their language wouldn't be lost.
In February 2026, Nahuat launched its own Wikipedia.
And in Nahuizalco, the town that rose up in 1932, the nest has a new building: seventeen children, Monday to Friday, and Saturday classes for all ages.
It was paid for by a Spanish city: Pamplona.
Why Pamplona?
They explain it themselves: in Navarre they know what it's like to watch a language retreat and bring it back with schools like this one, the ikastolas.
Since 2012, teacher-training students from Navarre have come to the nests for their internships.
If you go to El Salvador, these towns are one or two hours from the capital, on the Ruta de las Flores.
In Nahuizalco there's a night market and tule crafts.
And in Izalco, every January 22, the uprising is remembered.
If you meet someone who speaks Nahuat, now you know how to say hello: yek peyna, good morning.
From extermination to the anthem.
Under Bukele, the country has counted its Indigenous people and given them a day.
What is still waiting has a name: a word about 1932.
A law.
And Nahuat in the schools of Sonsonate.
The president who changed El Salvador…
will he change this too?
Meanwhile, the language heard in the Assembly is kept alive by a few grandmothers.
And five-year-old children.
There are more peoples who were nearly wiped off the map.
Here are their stories.
